title: A difficulty set before use is a prior
statement: Treat any difficulty, threshold or cut score set before learners have answered as a labelled prior, and replace it with live response data.
example: Estimating one item's difficulty with reasonable precision needs at least 100 to 200 responses, and at about 10 students per course even 100 takes 10 to 20 cohorts.
detail: A diagnostic BrainLift worked through on AP courses notes that estimating one item's difficulty with reasonable precision needs at minimum 100-200 responses, that at about 10 students per course it takes 10-20 cohorts to reach 100, and so parameters must come from judgment and structural defaults (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`, lines 382-384). Its cold-start section, drawing on published studies, ranks a model's direct rating as the weakest approach (often r ≈ 0.4–0.6), behind feature-based models (r ≈ 0.7–0.87 with ≥100 calibrated items) and placement against 3–5 calibrated anchors, distrusts predictions that swing under small wording changes, and requires every pre-use value to carry a provenance label such as 'pre-use predicted, N=0' (lines 3172-3196). The reading courses' standard says the same: predicted difficulty is a prior with method, population, provenance and uncertainty, which live data must eventually replace (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/standards/student-course-quality/sources/knowledge-bot/kb-0164-g3-v2-feedback-agent-routing.qmd`, lines 97-98). Estimate a pre-use difficulty from item features or calibrated anchors rather than a model's own rating, record its method, sample size and uncertainty, and set no cut score on it.
against: Both stronger methods need calibrated items that a new course doesn't have, which leaves rubric scoring of difficulty drivers for the cold start (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`, line 3186); and in one assessment bank all 650 items carry assigned, uncalibrated difficulties, so nobody knows how hard any single item actually is for students (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/05_LIMITATIONS.md`, line 11). Simulation suggests a well-built adaptive engine tolerates the guess, keeping reliability at or above 0.85, though with less precision than after calibration. The one internal case offered for it is unsettled: two simulation misses were traced to difficulties assigned by hand rather than estimated from responses (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0080-map-proxy-case-for-approval-2026-07-02-incept-map-proxy-approval-package.qmd`), but a later self-reported run on a bigger bank (786 items vs 650) reported RMSE 3.20 against the earlier 4.12 (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0086-round2-feedback-brainlifts-2026-07-09.qmd`). The 200-response line is the doctrine's example, not a calibrated threshold. Simulated students are best used only as a supplementary signal, and the advice to place a new item against calibrated anchors is the BrainLift's own view, with no study cited for it (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0163-cold-start-item-difficulty-estimation.qmd`).
